title: 7.6 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can go beyond today's lesson: solve an inequality and graph its solution set on a number line in trickier cases, and explain WHY it works.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: Detective Ortiz is reviewing a stakeout log. The team's rule is that a suspect's vehicle must be parked for more than 20 minutes before they radio for backup, so the rule is m > 20, where m is minutes parked. Test a few values: is m = 15 a rule-breaker? Is m = 20? Is m = 25? What do you notice about which values of m satisfy m > 20, and what do you wonder about how many different values could make the rule true?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Surveillance Van Budget
revealWordProblem.text: Detective Reyes can spend at most $85 on gas for her surveillance van this week. She has already spent $52. Write an inequality for the additional amount g she can still spend, solve it, and describe how you would graph the solution set on a number line.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The inequality is 52 + g ≤ 85. Subtracting 52 from both sides: g ≤ 85 − 52 = 33. Since ≤ includes the boundary, the graph has a closed circle at 33, shaded to the left (toward smaller values), showing that Detective Reyes can spend $33 or less on additional gas this week.

turnAndTalk.question: Solving an inequality and solving an equation both isolate the variable. What is the same about your steps, and what is different about the answer you get?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Solving an inequality gives a range of solutions, not one number.

stems.en: The steps are the same because I ___ to ___ the variable.
stems.es: Los pasos son iguales porque ___ para ___ la variable.

stems.en: The answer is different because an inequality has ___.
stems.es: La respuesta es diferente porque una desigualdad tiene ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students note both use inverse operations to isolate the variable, but an inequality's solution is many values (a range) while an equation's is a single value.
turnAndTalk.extend: Predict: after you solve an inequality, how will the graph look different from graphing the solution to an equation? Justify.
extendStems: The inequality graph shows ___ while an equation shows ___.

turnAndTalk.question: When would solving an inequality help you stay within a real-life limit?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Inequalities describe rules where many amounts are allowed up to a limit.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students give a real budget/time/capacity limit and explain that the inequality's solution set shows all amounts that keep them within the limit.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 7.6. You've got the basics — now let's push on it: harder cases, a second strategy, and always the question "how do you KNOW?"

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do I solve an inequality and then graph it?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Solve with inverse operations, then graph the solution set: open circle for < or >, closed for ≤ or ≥. — and you can explain WHY, and predict when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Solve x + 3 > 53. The inverse of adding 3 is subtracting 3.
I subtract 3 from both sides: x + 3 − 3 > 53 − 3, so x > 50.
The symbol > does not include 50, so I use an open circle at 50.
'Greater than' shades right. Check: x = 60 gives 60 + 3 = 63 > 53. True!

weDo.title: Generalize it
lines: Start from what you know: Solve x − 5 ≤ 8. What is the inverse of subtracting 5?
Now predict: what happens with much bigger numbers, or numbers that share no common factors? Make a prediction, then check it.

youDo.title: Take the challenge
lines: Work the challenge problems below. For each one, be ready to justify your answer to a skeptic.
If you finish early: find a second strategy, or a case where it would break.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Solve each inequality using inverse operations, then graph the solution on the number line. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.
hints: First solve the inequality just like an equation — use inverse operations on both sides. Then graph the result.
Remember: open circle for < and >, closed circle for ≤ and ≥. Shade in the direction of the solution values.
explore.label: Solve each inequality, then graph the solution on the number line.

discourse.prompt: How is solving an inequality similar to and different from solving an equation?
discourse.sentenceFrame: Solving an inequality is like solving an equation because I still use ___, but it is different because the answer is ___ instead of ___.

onLevel.stem: Is x = 5 a solution to x + 4 > 12?
choices: No, because 5 + 4 = 9, and 9 is not greater than 12
onLevel.explanation: Substitute: 5 + 4 = 9. Since 9 > 12 is false, x = 5 is NOT a solution.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: 'Is 5 a solution?' means: substitute 5 for x and see whether the statement comes out TRUE.
Replace x with 5 and compute the left side completely. Then compare that result to 12 honestly — is it really greater?
Compute 5 + 4 first. Then ask: is that total greater than 12? Your yes-or-no needs the correct REASON attached to it.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Catch the Open vs. Closed Circle Mistake
onLevel.correctWork: The solving is correct: x ≥ 13. But the symbol ≥ means 'greater than OR equal to,' so 13 IS a solution and must be included. Use a CLOSED circle at 13 (not open), then shade right.
hints: Does the symbol ≥ include the boundary value 13, or leave it out?
≥ and ≤ use a closed circle; only < and > use an open circle. Here use a closed circle at 13.

extending.title: Find the Solving Error
extending.correctWork: The inverse of subtracting 8 is ADDING 8, not subtracting. Add 8 to both sides: x ≥ 15 + 8 = 23. Graph: closed circle at 23, shade right.
hints: The equation has − 8. What is the inverse of subtracting 8?
To undo − 8, you add 8 to both sides: x ≥ 15 + 8 = 23.

extending.prompt: A detective has a budget of at most $100 for supplies. She already spent $37 on gloves. Write an inequality for the remaining amount r she can spend, solve it, graph it, and name three possible values for r.
extending.sentenceFrame: Inequality: 37 + r ≤ ___. Solving: r ≤ ___ − 37 = ___. Graph: ___ circle at ___, shade ___. Three possible values: ___.
extending.hint: Use a strategy or example from the lesson to help you explain your answer.
hints: 'At most $100' caps the TOTAL: the $37 already spent plus the remaining amount r must stay within 100.
Model it as 37 + r ≤ 100, then subtract 37 from both sides. 'At most' means the boundary IS allowed — remember that for the circle.
Compute 100 − 37 to find r's boundary. Then choose any three amounts at or below that boundary as your example values.

extending.label: Solve each inequality and verify by testing two values.
extending.hint: Work through each row step by step, checking your answer after each one.
hints: Two jobs per row: solve the inequality, then plug x = 5 and x = 20 into the ORIGINAL to see which value satisfies it.
Solve with inverse operations — the symbol keeps its direction. For each test, substitute, compute the left side, then judge the comparison.
Row 1: subtract 8 from both sides of x + 8 > 15. Then test x = 5: compute 5 + 8 and ask whether it really beats 15.

optional.stem: Clue 1: Which value is a solution of x > 7?
optional.explanation: A solution makes x > 7 true. Substitute each: 9 > 7 is true, but 7 > 7, 5 > 7, and 3 > 7 are all false. So 9 is the solution that opens the gate.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

optional.stem: Clue 2: Is 5 a solution of x ≤ 5?
choices: No, because 5 is not less than 5
No, because ≤ means only smaller numbers
Yes, but only because 5 is odd
optional.explanation: Substitute x = 5 into x ≤ 5: 5 ≤ 5 is true because ≤ means 'less than OR equal to.' The boundary value 5 IS a solution, so the gate opens.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

optional.stem: Final gate — describe the solution set. The vault rule is x > 7. What does the solution set mean?
choices: All numbers greater than 7, like 8, 9, 10, … (but NOT 7 itself)
optional.explanation: The solution set is every value that makes x > 7 true. That means all numbers greater than 7, such as 8, 9, 10, and beyond. Because > does not include the boundary, 7 itself is NOT in the solution set.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Solve and Graph Inequalities is shading the number line in the wrong direction after solving. For example, a student solves x + 4 > 10 correctly to get x > 6, but then shades LEFT toward smaller numbers instead of RIGHT toward greater numbers. The shading direction always matches the solved symbol, not the original problem: '>' and '≥' shade right (greater numbers), '<' and '≤' shade left (smaller numbers) — check this AFTER you solve, not before. To catch this mistake, substitute one shaded value and one unshaded value back into the original inequality: the shaded value should make it true, and the unshaded value should make it false.

optionalActivity.name: Inequality Escape Path
optionalActivity.intro: Challenge — prove it: Detective, each value is a clue — only true solutions clear the next gate and lead you out of the vault. Convince a skeptic your answer is right.

diagram.title: Money She Still Needs
diagram.caption: Solve 48 + s ≥ 75 to get s ≥ 27: the closed circle at 27 is included, and every value to the right (like 30 or 40) is a solution, while 20 is not enough.

connect.scenario: A detective needs at least $75 for a surveillance camera. She has already saved $48. The inequality 48 + s ≥ 75 represents how much more money s she needs.
connect.promptQuestion: How much more does the detective need? How did you solve and graph this inequality?
connect.prompt: The detective needs at least $__ more because 48 + s ≥ 75 means s ≥ 75 − ___ = ___.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Solve and describe the graph: x + 5 < 11
choices: x < 6; open circle at 6, shade left
x < 16; open circle at 16, shade left
x ≤ 6; closed circle at 6, shade left
x > 6; open circle at 6, shade right
exitTicket.explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides: x < 11 − 5 = 6. Open circle at 6 (not included), shade left. ✓
choiceFeedback: You added 5 — subtract 5 from both sides instead.
'<' is strict, so use an open circle, not a closed one.
Subtracting keeps the '<' direction — shade left, not right.
hints: Two parts here: first solve for x with an inverse operation, then describe the circle and the shading for your result.
Subtract 5 from both sides — the < keeps its direction. A strict < also tells you whether the boundary point is included.
Compute 11 − 5 for the boundary, decide the circle from the strict <, then test a small value like x = 2 to find the shading side.

smallGroup.label: Challenge
smallGroup.who: Pull students who showed mastery on the formative check and are ready to extend.
moves: Launch the challenge fast — skip the re-teach, they don't need it.
Step back. Let them wrestle; protect the productive struggle.
Ask "How do you know?" and "Can you show it a second way?" more than you explain.
Push for a generalization: when does this hold, and when would it break?
Close by having one student justify a claim to the group.
